title: Common sense key ; Great to get answers but latest inquest unnecessary
article: When someone dies for reasons that are unclear, we want to know why.
That's a big reason why we have inquests -- to try to explain the unexplained.
Just as important, if not more, inquests are a tool to help prevent similar deaths from happening again.

Inquests can illuminate what might otherwise remain hidden and bring about change. One of the most prominent examples is the 1996 inquest into baby deaths at Health Sciences Centre. The 30-month inquest shone a blistering light on the hospital's pediatric heart unit and its former chief surgeon, Dr. Jonah Odim. A 500-plus page inquest report by then-associate chief judge Murray Sinclair, and the recommendations it contained, would reverberate within the health system for years.
At the opposite end of the spectrum, there's the case of Randy George Krasnesky. He died March 16, 2007, after Selkirk RCMP pulled him over on suspicion of drug trafficking.
There's no mystery why Krasnesky died. He died because he had swallowed a condom filled with enough cocaine to fell a moose.

I don't mean to be cruel or insensitive here. I'm sure the people who loved or cared for Krasnesky would sleep better thinking he was a victim of forces outside his control and not the master of his demise.
The simple truth is Krasnesky died as a result of his own foolhardy behaviour.
But because he died while in police custody, chief medical examiner Dr. Thambirajah Balachandra had no choice but to order an inquest, mandatory under the Fatality Inquiries Act.
The inquest heard Krasnesky showed no signs of medical distress when police first pulled his vehicle over.

Once arrested and seated in the back of a police cruiser, Krasnesky complained he was ill, demanded he be taken to a hospital, and then vomited on himself and went into convulsions before losing consciousness. Police removed Krasnesky from the cruiser, placed him in a "recovery position" and called for an ambulance. He died in Selkirk's hospital an hour later.
An autopsy determined Krasnesky died of an acute cocaine overdose after a drug-filled condom ruptured inside him.
Balachandra told the inquest first responders had a window of just five minutes to save Krasnesky after he overdosed.

"It would have been almost impossible to treat this patient given the amount of cocaine in his system," Balachandra testified, adding he's seen patients die after ingesting just 1/10 the cocaine Krasnesky did.
Unsurprisingly, Judge Michel Chartier concluded a 29-page inquest report released Sept. 29 by finding there was nothing he could recommend to prevent similar deaths from happening in the future.
The closest he came to a recommendation was to suggest Mounties regularly review their operations manual.

I don't fault anyone who participated in what was a mandatory process. But at the end of the day, what do we have to show for a five-day inquest that occupied the time of 16 witnesses, at least two lawyers, a judge and a court clerk? At a time when critics decry increasing court backlogs and a constant shortage of resources, it's not an unfair question.
I'm not suggesting the scales of justice be weighted with balance sheets, just some common sense. We didn't need an inquest to tell us police and paramedics played no role in Krasnesky's death.
Was the Kraskesky inquest time (and money) well spent? You be the judge.
